Indignant

/in-DIG-nuhnt/ - the stress falls on DIG · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Indignant means feeling or showing anger at something unjust or unfair.

Maribel came back to a ticket on the one car on the block with a valid permit, and stood indignant in the street, waving it after the departing scooter.

Worked Example

Mrs. Okoye's rhubarb pie was disqualified twenty minutes before judging, for a rule about store-bought crusts that appears nowhere in the printed booklet. She did not cry and she did not shrug. She stood at the officials' table with the booklet open, reading the rules aloud, slowly, page by page, and asked the head judge to point to the one she had broken.

Indignant is the exact word because it names anger at unfairness in particular. She isn't merely disappointed at losing, and this isn't a tantrum; the heat comes from the injustice — a rule invented after the fact. Anger says how she feels; indignant says why the feeling is earned.

How Indignant Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

outraged

outraged: the same anger at full boil

offended

offended: stung by a slight; indignant adds the sense that something unfair has been done

Antonyms

unruffled

unruffled: calm, feathers unstirred

gratified

gratified: pleased at how things went

How Strong Is It? — annoyed → indignant → incensed

annoyed vs. indignant

annoyed vs. indignant: Annoyed is the small coin of irritation, spent on traffic and slow elevators; indignant is anger with a wrong at the bottom of it.

incensed vs. indignant

incensed vs. indignant: Incensed goes past indignant — the anger has caught fire and stopped choosing its words.

Sort It Out

Now place each word on the right side of indignant.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — in-

Prefix — in-: not

Root — dign

Root — dign: worthy (Latin dignus)

Suffix — -ant

Suffix — -ant: inclined to

Put it together

Put it together: In- (not) + dign (worthy — Latin dignus) + -ant = treated as not worthy. Latin indignari meant to judge a thing beneath what someone deserves — unworthy treatment — and to burn at it. Indignant keeps the full circuit: an injustice done, a worth denied, and the anger that answers.

Use the root in a new word: dignity

Use the root in a new word: dignity: Dignity is the same root at peace — the worth a person carries, which unfair treatment insults.

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral

Indignant is anger with a case to make: something unfair happened, and the feeling knows it. Plain angry needs no reason; indignant supplies one. Its noun is this unit's indignation, and the pair travel together — an indignant customer, full of indignation. If no injustice is anywhere in sight, the honest word is just annoyed.
